Thesis and project work is available in areas such as autonomous systems, robot control and motion planning, and the program prepares graduates for industry roles and further study.
text:
I am writing in strong support of Grace Sharma's application to the MS in Robotics program at University of Minnesota, Twin Cities. I am a Principal Investigator and supervised Grace for 12 months in my research group, where she worked on a project in human-robot interaction. I have supervised about 20 researchers and interns over the past decade.

The first example that comes to mind is a project in which Grace developed a visual-servoing controller using OpenCV, and it positioned a gripper within 5 millimetres in 87% of trials. What stood out to me was that Grace defined success in advance, tested her own assumptions and reported the limitations honestly, including the cases in which the approach did not work. I did not have to ask for that rigour.

A second example came later. Grace implemented an A* motion planner for a mobile robot in C++, and it reduced path length by 41% compared with the baseline. When a result looked too good to be true, Grace insisted on re-running the analysis from scratch and found an error that would otherwise have gone unnoticed.

Grace is among the better engineers I have worked with.

In a disagreement over the direction of the work, Grace presented data rather than opinion, listened carefully to the alternative, and ended up combining the two approaches. When my feedback on her first draft was critical, Grace came back the next morning with a revised plan and a list of precise questions, and the second version was far stronger.

I believe the match with the MS in Robotics program is strong. Her work in human-robot interaction and preparation in kinematics equip her for courses such as State Estimation and Robot Kinematics and Dynamics, and her interest in state estimation and especially in Autonomous Systems gives her a clear direction. I expect her to contribute to class discussion and to the wider community.

Grace has my strongest recommendation. I am certain that she will be an asset to your program and a credit to her cohort, and I would welcome a call if it would help your committee.

Sincerely,
Dr. Sneha Hussain
Principal Investigator

text:
I have been interested in computer vision for several years. Over time my work has repeatedly pointed me back to it, and I now want to study it in a structured way.

I graduated in Sociology with a GPA of 3.33 on a 4.0 scale. My coursework included computer vision and probabilistic reasoning, and I enjoyed the practical parts of the curriculum. Because my degree was in Sociology, I also took some online courses in computer vision.

After graduating I spent 5 years at an investment bank as an analyst. That work taught me how quickly a model and its assumptions have to be defended, and it kept bringing me back to problems such as manual review queues that should have been triaged by a model. At the investment bank I built an image-based defect detector using a convolutional network, and it reached 97% recall on a held-out set of 1200 images. I later developed a demand model using gradient boosting and careful feature engineering, and it reduced forecast error by 24% against the incumbent method. These projects taught me to measure results before claiming success and to document decisions so that other people can build on them.

Alongside my work, I contributed to research in sequential decision-making. I co-authored two papers, one of them as first author, and my responsibility was designing and running the experiments. Seeing reviewers challenge our assumptions taught me to document methods so that others can reproduce them.

I also took part in college and workplace activities and was a member of the student consulting group.

Working on manual review queues that should have been triaged by a model also showed me what I still lack. I can use scikit-learn and Docker to solve a well-defined problem, but I cannot yet justify my choices in probabilistic reasoning from first principles or defend them to a sceptical expert. Closing that gap requires structured training, rigorous feedback and time to work on problems in depth, which is hard to get while delivering projects on a deadline.

I am applying to the MS in Artificial Intelligence program at University of Maryland, College Park because it matches the direction I want to take. As I understand the curriculum, it combines Computer Vision, Probabilistic Graphical Models and Reinforcement Learning in a way that fits the skills I need to build. I am particularly drawn to the department's emphasis on language understanding, which connects directly to my earlier work. In my first year I would plan to take Computer Vision early, and use a project in Deep Learning to test whether trustworthy and ethical AI is the area I want to pursue in depth. I also value the chance to learn alongside peers from different backgrounds, since my best work has always come from teams that disagreed productively.

In the short term, I plan to build depth in computer vision through coursework and a project connected to sequential decision-making, then move into a machine learning engineer position. Within 7 years of graduating, I aim to pursue applied research in AI that is accountable to the people it affects. This direction follows from my experience in investment banking and my work on computer vision, and I believe it is realistic given what I have already built.

I will bring to the program a record of building things, measuring whether they work, and learning from the results. I am ready to contribute to classroom discussion, to group projects and to the wider community from my first semester.

It was the first time I understood that embedded systems decides whether a system, or a decision, can be trusted, and I have organised my studies and career around that idea ever since.

I completed my undergraduate degree in Psychology with a GPA of 3.13 on a 4.0 scale. Coming from Psychology, I knew I would have to build technical depth deliberately. Alongside my job I completed 3 additional courses in embedded systems and communication systems, and I finished a capstone project on control systems in which I worked with a small team to build and test a prototype, which convinced me this was not a passing interest.

After graduating I spent 6 years at a private equity firm as an investment associate. That work taught me how much value depends on diligence that is both quantitative and fast, and it kept bringing me back to problems such as systems that were unstable at the edge of their operating range. At the private equity firm I modelled a PID control loop for a motor in MATLAB and tested it on hardware, and it cut settling time by 26% with no overshoot. I later built a maximum-power-point tracker for a solar panel around a microcontroller, and it raised harvested energy by 27% over 21 test days. Each of these projects reinforced the same lesson: careful measurement matters more than clever ideas, and clear communication is part of the work.

Not every project went as planned. When I designed a digital filter on an FPGA in Verilog, my first approach failed because the data were far noisier than I had assumed. I rebuilt the core of the approach, added tests for the failure case, and shared the revised plan openly with the team, and in the end it improved signal-to-noise ratio by 32 dB while using under 5% of the logic. The episode taught me to look for disconfirming evidence early, and to treat a failed attempt as information rather than embarrassment.

I have also been involved in three papers in control and power systems.

Outside work I coordinated a hackathon with 3 teammates and a budget of $200, and learning to resolve disagreements between volunteers prepared me for the group work I expect in a graduate programme.

A prototype sensor I built produced beautiful readings on my own wrist and useless ones on a patient, and understanding why made me realise that medical engineering begins with the person, not the circuit. From that point I stopped treating computational biology as a side interest and began building my career around it.

I completed my undergraduate degree in Electrical Engineering with a GPA of 3.23 on a 4.0 scale. Coursework in computational biology, medical imaging and physiological signals gave me the analytical foundations I still rely on, and in my final-year project on biomechanics I worked with a small team to build and test a prototype, which showed me how much there was still to learn. I also served as a teaching assistant for a course in medical imaging, where explaining concepts to 90 students showed me which ideas I understood and which I had only memorised.

After graduating I spent 5 years at a public-sector agency as a programme analyst. That work taught me how limited resources make rigorous evaluation essential, and it kept bringing me back to problems such as materials that failed mechanical testing too early. At the public-sector agency I developed a signal-processing pipeline for ECG data in MATLAB, and it improved arrhythmia detection sensitivity to 92% on 200 recordings. I later tested a polymer scaffold for cell growth through 800 mechanical and degradation trials, and it identified a formulation that retained 97% of its strength after four weeks. Looking back, the most valuable lesson was that the technical solution is rarely the hardest part; getting people to trust and adopt it takes just as much care.

Not every project went as planned. When I designed a low-cost pulse-oximetry prototype using an Arduino and a photodiode sensor, my first approach failed because my first design did not hold up beyond 1200 cases. I spent 4 weeks testing alternatives, writing down what each one taught me, and asking two senior colleagues to challenge my approach, and in the end it agreed with a clinical reference device within 3 percent across 500 readings. The episode taught me to look for disconfirming evidence early, and to treat a failed attempt as information rather than embarrassment.

I have also been involved in four papers in medical devices.

I have mentored 4 junior colleagues over the past two years, and helping one of them move from basic spreadsheets to writing reliable scripts was among the most rewarding things I have done.

Working on materials that failed mechanical testing too early also showed me what I still lack. I can use SolidWorks and R to solve a well-defined problem, but I cannot yet justify my choices in medical imaging from first principles or defend them to a sceptical expert. Closing that gap requires structured training, rigorous feedback and time to work on problems in depth, which is hard to get while delivering projects on a deadline.

I am applying to the MS in Biomedical Engineering program at Cornell University with a specialization in Computational Biology because it matches the direction I want to take. As I understand the curriculum, it combines Computational Biology, Biomechanics and Medical Instrumentation in a way that fits the skills I need to build. I am particularly drawn to the Computational Biology track, because it connects directly to the problems I met at the public-sector agency. In my first year I would plan to take Computational Biology early, and use a project in Medical Imaging to test whether computational physiology is the area I want to pursue in depth. I also value the chance to learn alongside peers from different backgrounds, since my best work has always come from teams that disagreed productively. I have also looked closely at how the program is structured, and I like that it lets students combine coursework with applied project work. I have already begun preparing by reviewing material in medical imaging and physiological signals, so that I can engage with advanced content from the first week.

After my degree, I want to work as a biomedical engineer and contribute to projects related to computational biology.

I come to this program with specific questions, a record of finishing what I start, and a clear sense of how the degree fits into my plans. I hope to be given the chance to continue that work with you.

I have been interested in analog circuits for several years. Over time my work has repeatedly pointed me back to it, and I now want to study it in a structured way.

I completed my undergraduate degree in Economics with a GPA of 3.07 on a 4.0 scale. Coming from Economics, I knew I would have to build technical depth deliberately. Alongside my job I completed 3 additional courses in analog circuits and power electronics, and I finished a capstone project on embedded systems in which I worked with a small team to build and test a prototype, which convinced me this was not a passing interest.

After graduating I spent 5 years at a management consulting firm as a consultant. That work taught me how often client decisions rest on assumptions nobody has tested, and it kept bringing me back to problems such as circuits that wasted power. At the management consulting firm I modelled a PID control loop for a motor in MATLAB and tested it on hardware, and it cut settling time by 29% with no overshoot. I later built a maximum-power-point tracker for a solar panel around a microcontroller, and it raised harvested energy by 41% over 28 test days. Looking back, the most valuable lesson was that the technical solution is rarely the hardest part; getting people to trust and adopt it takes just as much care.

Not every project went as planned. When I designed a digital filter on an FPGA in Verilog, my first approach failed because a key assumption turned out to be wrong. I spent 7 weeks testing alternatives, writing down what each one taught me, and asking two senior colleagues to challenge my approach, and in the end it improved signal-to-noise ratio by 33 dB while using under 7% of the logic. The episode taught me to look for disconfirming evidence early, and to treat a failed attempt as information rather than embarrassment.

Alongside my work, I contributed to research in VLSI and low-power design. I co-authored two papers, two as first author, and my responsibility was building the data pipeline and the evaluation. Seeing reviewers challenge our assumptions taught me to document methods so that others can reproduce them.

I also took part in college and workplace activities and was a member of the student consulting group.

I am applying to the MS in Electrical Engineering program at University of California, Davis because it matches the direction I want to take. As I understand the curriculum, it combines Embedded Systems, Linear Control Systems and Power Electronics in a way that fits the skills I need to build. In my first year I would plan to take Embedded Systems early, and use a project in Wireless Communications to test whether communications and signal processing is the area I want to pursue in depth. I also value the chance to learn alongside peers from different backgrounds, since my best work has always come from teams that disagreed productively. I expect to learn as much from classmates as from instructors, and I intend to contribute to study groups and student organisations. I have already begun preparing by reviewing material in power electronics and embedded systems, so that I can engage with advanced content from the first week.

In the short term, I plan to build depth in analog circuits through coursework and a project connected to VLSI and low-power design, then move into a electrical engineer position. Within 5 years of graduating, I aim to lead design of efficient power and communication systems. This direction follows from my experience in consulting and my work on analog circuits, and I believe it is realistic given what I have already built.

What I offer is a habit of testing my own assumptions, a willingness to ask for help early, and several years of practice turning vague problems into measurable ones. I would be glad to put those habits to work with my classmates.

Over the time I have known Aisha, her growth has been striking. Early on, her explanations were correct but hard to follow; within a year she was presenting power electronics results to senior audiences with clarity and calm.

I do not make comparisons lightly. Among the roughly 300 engineers I have worked with in 20 years, Aisha ranks in the top 2 percent, and in analytical ability and independence I would place her alongside the best.

When my feedback on her first draft was critical, Aisha came back the next morning with a revised plan and a list of precise questions, and the second version was far stronger. Aisha regularly mentored newer colleagues, and 6 of them told me independently that she was the person they turned to when they were stuck.

I expect her to contribute to class discussion and to the wider community.

Dr. Wei Evans
Associate Professor

I have been interested in kinematics for several years. Over time my work has repeatedly pointed me back to it, and I now want to study it in a structured way.

I completed my undergraduate degree in Chemistry with a GPA of 3.12 on a 4.0 scale. Coursework in kinematics, state estimation and human-robot interaction gave me the analytical foundations I still rely on, and in my final-year project on motion planning I worked with a small team to build and test a prototype, which showed me how much there was still to learn. I also served as a teaching assistant for a course in state estimation, where explaining concepts to 90 students showed me which ideas I understood and which I had only memorised.

After graduating I spent 5 years at an investment bank as an analyst. That work taught me how quickly a model and its assumptions have to be defended, and it kept bringing me back to problems such as robots that worked in the lab and failed in the corridor. At the investment bank I developed a visual-servoing controller using OpenCV, and it positioned a gripper within 5 millimetres in 96% of trials. I later built a line-following and obstacle-avoiding robot using ROS and a LiDAR sensor, and it completed 200 consecutive course runs with no collisions. These projects taught me to measure results before claiming success and to document decisions so that other people can build on them.

Not every project went as planned. When I implemented an A* motion planner for a mobile robot in C++, my first approach failed because a key assumption turned out to be wrong. I spent 7 weeks testing alternatives, writing down what each one taught me, and asking two senior colleagues to challenge my approach, and in the end it reduced path length by 23% compared with the baseline. The episode taught me to look for disconfirming evidence early, and to treat a failed attempt as information rather than embarrassment.

Alongside my work, I contributed to research in motion planning. I co-authored three papers, one of them as first author, and my responsibility was building the data pipeline and the evaluation. The work taught me to separate what a result shows from what I hoped it would show.

I have mentored 9 junior colleagues over the past two years, and helping one of them move from basic spreadsheets to writing reliable scripts was among the most rewarding things I have done.

I am applying to the MS in Robotics program at University of Connecticut with a specialization in Human-Robot Interaction because it matches the direction I want to take. As I understand the curriculum, it combines Motion Planning, Robot Control and Robot Kinematics and Dynamics in a way that fits the skills I need to build. I am particularly drawn to the Human-Robot Interaction track, because it connects directly to the problems I met at the investment bank. In my first year I would plan to take Motion Planning early, and use a project in State Estimation to test whether autonomous systems is the area I want to pursue in depth. I also value the chance to learn alongside peers from different backgrounds, since my best work has always come from teams that disagreed productively. I expect to learn as much from classmates as from instructors, and I intend to contribute to study groups and student organisations. I have already begun preparing by reviewing material in state estimation and human-robot interaction, so that I can engage with advanced content from the first week.

In the short term, I plan to complete a capstone or thesis in kinematics, take a summer internship focused on state estimation, and then join a team as a robotics engineer. Within 5 years of graduating, I aim to lead development of reliable autonomous systems. This direction follows from my experience in investment banking and my work on kinematics, and I believe it is realistic given what I have already built. I have already started preparing for that path: I completed 3 online modules in human-robot interaction, I read widely on human-robot interaction, and I keep short notes on what I learn so that I can explain it to others.

I will bring to the program a record of building things, measuring whether they work, and learning from the results. I am ready to contribute to classroom discussion, to group projects and to the wider community from my first semester.

I have been interested in manufacturing processes for several years. Over time my work has repeatedly pointed me back to it, and I now want to study it in a structured way.

I graduated in Management Information Systems with a GPA of 3.51 on a 4.0 scale. My coursework included manufacturing processes and solid mechanics, and I enjoyed the practical parts of the curriculum. Because my degree was in Management Information Systems, I also took some online courses in manufacturing processes.

After graduating I spent 6 years at a mid-sized company as an operations analyst. That work taught me how process gaps quietly drain time and money, and it kept bringing me back to problems such as cooling systems that used more energy than they needed to. At the mid-sized company I modelled a shell-and-tube heat exchanger in ANSYS Fluent across 60 baffle configurations, and it found a design that improved heat transfer by 38%. I later analysed a vehicle chassis using finite element analysis, and it cut mass by 24% while keeping the safety factor above 2. These projects taught me to measure results before claiming success and to document decisions so that other people can build on them.

Not every project went as planned. When I optimised the CNC parameters for a machining operation across 40 components, my first approach failed because a key assumption turned out to be wrong. I spent 3 weeks testing alternatives, writing down what each one taught me, and asking two senior colleagues to challenge my approach, and in the end it reduced scrap by 31%. The episode taught me to look for disconfirming evidence early, and to treat a failed attempt as information rather than embarrassment.

Alongside my work, I contributed to research in advanced manufacturing. I co-authored three papers, and my responsibility was designing and running the experiments. The work taught me to separate what a result shows from what I hoped it would show.

I have mentored 9 junior colleagues over the past two years, and helping one of them move from basic spreadsheets to writing reliable scripts was among the most rewarding things I have done.

Working on cooling systems that used more energy than they needed to also showed me what I still lack. I can use ANSYS and MATLAB to solve a well-defined problem, but I cannot yet justify my choices in solid mechanics from first principles or defend them to a sceptical expert. Closing that gap requires structured training, rigorous feedback and time to work on problems in depth, which is hard to get while delivering projects on a deadline.

I am applying to the MS in Mechanical Engineering program at Rice University with a specialization in Design because it matches the direction I want to take. As I understand the curriculum, it combines Advanced Heat Transfer, Mechanical Vibrations and Finite Element Analysis in a way that fits the skills I need to build. I am particularly drawn to the Design track, because it connects directly to the problems I met at the mid-sized company. In my first year I would plan to take Advanced Heat Transfer early, and use a project in Advanced Thermodynamics to test whether machine design is the area I want to pursue in depth. I also value the chance to learn alongside peers from different backgrounds, since my best work has always come from teams that disagreed productively. I expect to learn as much from classmates as from instructors, and I intend to contribute to study groups and student organisations. I have already begun preparing by reviewing material in solid mechanics and heat transfer, so that I can engage with advanced content from the first week.

After my degree, I want to work as a mechanical engineer and contribute to projects related to manufacturing processes.

I will bring to the program a record of building things, measuring whether they work, and learning from the results. I am ready to contribute to classroom discussion, to group projects and to the wider community from my first semester.

When a result looked too good to be true, Ishaan insisted on re-running the analysis from scratch and found an error that would otherwise have gone unnoticed.

I believe the match with the MS in Industrial Engineering program is strong. His work in healthcare operations and preparation in human factors equip him for courses such as Stochastic Models and Production Planning, and his interest in production planning and especially in Supply Chain gives him a clear direction. I expect him to contribute to class discussion and to the wider community.

Vice President

A pricing proposal I had spent weeks on was rejected in ten minutes because I could not explain the assumption behind one number, and I resolved never to be unprepared like that again. That experience made competitive strategy less of an abstract subject and more of a practical problem I wanted to solve properly.

I completed my undergraduate degree in English Literature with a GPA of 3.29 on a 4.0 scale. Coursework in competitive strategy, organisational behaviour and corporate finance gave me the analytical foundations I still rely on, and in my final-year project on operations management I worked with a small team to build and test a prototype, which showed me how much there was still to learn. I also served as a teaching assistant for a course in organisational behaviour, where explaining concepts to 40 students showed me which ideas I understood and which I had only memorised.

After graduating I spent 6 years at an investment bank as an analyst. That work taught me how quickly a model and its assumptions have to be defended, and it kept bringing me back to problems such as teams that lacked a shared view of the numbers. At the investment bank I led a pricing review across 200 product lines, and it lifted gross margin by 12% within two quarters. I later built a market-entry assessment from interviews with 200 customers, and it persuaded leadership to approve a pilot that reached 96% of its first-year target in six months. Looking back, the most valuable lesson was that the technical solution is rarely the hardest part; getting people to trust and adopt it takes just as much care.

Not every project went as planned. When I led a cost-reduction programme with a team of 3 analysts, my first approach failed because my first design did not hold up beyond 60 cases. I rebuilt the core of the approach, added tests for the failure case, and shared the revised plan openly with the team, and in the end it saved about $1200K a year without cutting service levels. The episode taught me to look for disconfirming evidence early, and to treat a failed attempt as information rather than embarrassment.

Alongside my work, I contributed to research in leadership and organisational change. I co-authored three papers, two as first author, and my responsibility was designing and running the experiments. Seeing reviewers challenge our assumptions taught me to document methods so that others can reproduce them.

Outside work I coordinated a community fundraising drive with 9 teammates and a budget of $120, and learning to resolve disagreements between volunteers prepared me for the group work I expect in a graduate programme.

Working on teams that lacked a shared view of the numbers also showed me what I still lack. I can use SQL and Tableau to solve a well-defined problem, but I cannot yet justify my choices in organisational behaviour from first principles or defend them to a sceptical expert. Closing that gap requires structured training, rigorous feedback and time to work on problems in depth, which is hard to get while delivering projects on a deadline.

I am applying to the MBA in Business Administration program at Boston University with a specialization in Finance because it matches the direction I want to take. As I understand the curriculum, it combines Managerial Accounting, Competitive Strategy and Operations Management in a way that fits the skills I need to build. I am particularly drawn to the Finance track, because it connects directly to the problems I met at the investment bank. In my first year I would plan to take Managerial Accounting early, and use a project in Corporate Finance to test whether sustainable business is the area I want to pursue in depth. I also value the chance to learn alongside peers from different backgrounds, since my best work has always come from teams that disagreed productively. The first example that comes to mind is a project in which Hannah developed a signal-processing pipeline for ECG data in MATLAB, and it improved arrhythmia detection sensitivity to 86% on 500 recordings. What stood out to me was that Hannah defined success in advance, tested her own assumptions and reported the limitations honestly, including the cases in which the approach did not work. I did not have to ask for that rigour.

A second example came later. Hannah tested a polymer scaffold for cell growth through 200 mechanical and degradation trials, and it identified a formulation that retained 92% of its strength after four weeks. In a disagreement over the direction of the work, Hannah presented data rather than opinion, listened carefully to the alternative, and ended up combining the two approaches.

Over the time I have known Hannah, her growth has been striking. Early on, her explanations were correct but hard to follow; within a year she was presenting computational biology results to senior audiences with clarity and calm. Hannah designed a low-cost pulse-oximetry prototype using an Arduino and a photodiode sensor, and it agreed with a clinical reference device within 3 percent across 150 readings. When a result looked too good to be true, Hannah insisted on re-running the analysis from scratch and found an error that would otherwise have gone unnoticed.

I do not make comparisons lightly. Among the roughly 50 students I have worked with in 12 years, Hannah ranks in the top 3 percent, and in analytical ability and independence I would place her alongside the best.

During a stressful deadline, Hannah noticed that a teammate was struggling and spent 4 evenings helping without being asked, so the whole team delivered on time. Hannah regularly mentored newer colleagues, and 5 of them told me independently that she was the person they turned to when they were stuck.

I believe the match with the MS in Biomedical Engineering program is strong. Her work in rehabilitation engineering and preparation in physiological signals equip her for courses such as Medical Imaging and Biomaterials, and her interest in biomechanics and especially in Biomechanics gives her a clear direction. I expect her to contribute to class discussion and to the wider community.

If I could offer only one sentence it would be this: admit Hannah, and you will not regret it. I am happy to discuss her candidacy in more detail.

Sincerely,
Dr. Nisha Malhotra
Senior Research Scientist
